core_question: How do I stop pipes from banging loudly when a faucet or valve shuts off?
answer_summary: Install a water hammer arrestor (an air-cushioned fitting) near the offending valve or appliance to absorb the pressure shock, or drain the plumbing system to restore air cushions in the pipes.
persona: impatient and curt; writing terse one-liners

messages.content: Pipes keep banging. Faucet shuts off, BANG. Loud. Fix it.
That banging sound—does it happen the moment a valve closes, or does it keep goin for a bit after?
Right when it shuts. What's the solution?
So the pressure changes instantly when the valve closes—what do you think that pressure suddenly has nowhere to go?
When water pressure hits a closed valve and can't move forward, what happens to that force—does it disappear?
It bounces back or something? I dunno.
Right—so that rebound force is sometimes called a shock wave? And to absorb that shock, would you need something hard and rigid, or something that can cushion it?
Right—and in your plumbing system, what naturally acts like a cushion in the pipes when air gets trapped in there?
Air pockets? Like the air that's supposed to be there?
Yes—so if those air pockets can get absorbed into the water and used up over time, what do you think it would take to bring that cushioning back into the system?
